# Discounted Cash Flow Valuation {#sec-dcf}

This chapter teaches you to value a company from the cash it is expected to produce: how to measure free cash flow, choose a discount rate, forecast growth that is paid for with reinvestment, close the model with a terminal value, and turn enterprise value into a value per share. Sources are credited in footnotes and listed at the end of the chapter. "Example Co." figures are invented for teaching and continue the running example from @sec-fsa.

| **Section** | **Topic** | **Main question** |
|---------------|--------------------------|-------------------------------|
| 1 | The logic of DCF valuation | What is value, and which cash flow goes with which discount rate? |
| 2 | Free cash flow to the firm | How much cash does the business produce for all of its investors? |
| 3 | The discount rate | What return do investors require for the risk in those cash flows? |
| 4 | Growth, reinvestment and the forecast | How fast can the firm grow, and what must it spend to get there? |
| 5 | Terminal value | What is the firm worth after the forecast ends? |
| 6 | From enterprise value to value per share | What belongs to the common shareholder? |
| 7 | Sensitivity, implied expectations and common errors | How far can the answer be trusted? |

Sections 1 to 3 set up the three ingredients (cash flow, discount rate, horizon), Sections 4 and 5 supply the forecast and its end point, Section 6 completes the valuation of Example Co., and Section 7 tests it. Each section ends with review questions and a note on the related CFA readings. The Forecasting chapter supplies the operating forecast that feeds this chapter, and the Cost of Capital chapter supplies the discount rate; Sections 3 and 4 show where the three fit together.

## Section 1. The Logic of DCF Valuation {.unnumbered}

### Learning objectives {.unnumbered}

- State what intrinsic value is and why it depends on the size, timing and risk of cash flows.

- Name the four inputs of every DCF model.

- Distinguish firm (enterprise) valuation from equity valuation and say when each is the better choice.

- Apply the consistency principle: match the cash flow to the discount rate.

- Explain why a valuation is a story that has been turned into numbers.

### 1.1 Value comes from cash flows {.unnumbered}

The intrinsic value of an asset that produces cash is the present value of the cash it is expected to produce over its life, discounted at a rate that reflects the risk of receiving it:^[Aswath Damodaran, "Intrinsic Valuation," valuation course slides, Session 2, NYU Stern, <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/pdfiles/valonlineslides/session2.pdf>; and "Basics of DCF Valuation," equity valuation notes, <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/pdfiles/eqnotes/basics.pdf>.]

$$
\text{Value} = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{E(CF_t)}{(1+r)^t}
$$

Two propositions follow. An asset has value only if its expected cash flows are positive at some point in its life, and early losses are acceptable if later cash flows are large enough. Between two assets, the one that pays sooner is worth more, although a later stream can make up for the delay by being larger or growing faster. If an action changes neither the expected cash flows nor their risk, it cannot change value.

Risk can enter the model in two ways: by raising the discount rate above the risk-free rate (the approach used in this chapter), or by replacing each expected cash flow with a smaller certainty equivalent and discounting at the risk-free rate. Uncertainty is not a reason to skip the estimate. It is the reason the estimate must come with a range.

### 1.2 The four inputs {.unnumbered}

Every DCF model, however elaborate, needs four things:^[Damodaran, "Basics of DCF Valuation," <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/pdfiles/eqnotes/basics.pdf>.]

| **Input** | **Question** | **Where it is built** |
|--------------------|------------------------------|--------------------|
| Cash flows | How much cash does the business produce after taxes and after reinvestment? | Section 2 |
| Discount rate | What return do the providers of capital require? | Section 3 |
| Expected growth | How fast do the cash flows grow, and how is that growth funded? | Section 4 |
| Closure | What happens after the explicit forecast ends? | Section 5 |

A firm may live forever, but nobody can forecast forever. Practice therefore splits value into a **forecast period** (typically five to ten years of explicit cash flows) and a **terminal value** that captures everything after it:

$$
\text{Value} = \sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} + \frac{\text{Terminal value}_N}{(1+r)^N}
$$

### 1.3 Firm valuation and equity valuation {.unnumbered}

The cash flows can be measured before or after payments to lenders, and the discount rate must follow:

| **Approach** | **Cash flow** | **Discount rate** | **Result** |
|------------------|-------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Dividend discount | Dividends (or dividends plus buybacks) | Cost of equity | Value of equity |
| Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) | Cash left after taxes, reinvestment and net debt flows | Cost of equity | Value of equity |
| Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) | Cash before debt payments, after taxes and reinvestment | Cost of capital (WACC) | Value of the firm's operating assets |

The firm approach values all claims at once and then subtracts the claims that are not equity. It is the better choice when leverage is unusually high or low, when it is expected to change over time, or when the whole business is being valued, as in a merger or a buyout. The equity approach is simpler when leverage is stable. The dividend approach works when dividends track free cash flow to equity over time, and is hard to replace for banks, where debt is raw material rather than financing and free cash flow is hard to define.^[Damodaran, valuation course slides, Spring 2023, Session 11, "Discounted Cash Flow Valuation," <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/podcasts/valspr23/session11slides.pdf>.] This chapter uses FCFF, which is also the approach in the capstone project.

#### The consistency principle {.unnumbered}

> **Never mix cash flows and discount rates.** Cash flows after debt payments are discounted at the cost of equity. Cash flows before debt payments are discounted at the cost of capital.

The following illustration shows what a mismatch does. A firm has a cost of equity of 13.625%, equity worth \$1,073 and debt of \$800 with an after-tax cost of 5%. Its WACC is 13.625% × (1,073 ÷ 1,873) + 5% × (800 ÷ 1,873) = 9.94%.^[Damodaran, "Basics of DCF Valuation," worked example, <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/pdfiles/eqnotes/basics.pdf>.]

| **Method** | **Value of firm or equity** | **Value of equity** | **Error** |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Equity cash flows at the cost of equity (13.625%) | n/a | \$1,073 | None |
| Firm cash flows at WACC (9.94%), less debt of \$800 | \$1,873 | \$1,073 | None |
| Equity cash flows at WACC (wrong) | n/a | \$1,248 | Overstated by \$175 |
| Firm cash flows at the cost of equity (wrong), less debt | \$1,613 | \$813 | Understated by \$260 |

Both consistent methods give the same equity value. Discounting equity cash flows at the lower WACC overstates value, and discounting firm cash flows at the higher cost of equity understates it.

### 1.4 The enterprise value balance sheet {.unnumbered}

A useful picture of what is being valued is the **enterprise value balance sheet**, which rearranges the accounting balance sheet so that the operating items sit on one side and the financing items on the other.^[Simon Benninga, *Financial Modeling*, 4th ed. (MIT Press, 2014), ch. 2, pp. 53–59.]

| **Operating side (valued by DCF)** | **Financing side (observed or estimated)** |
|-----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Net working capital, fixed assets, goodwill and other operating assets | Net financial debt, other liabilities, minority interest, equity |

Enterprise value (EV) is the value of the left-hand side. On the book values, Caterpillar's 2011 enterprise value is \$59.5 billion. Using the market value of its equity (624.7 million shares at \$90.60, or \$56.6 billion) and adding net debt of \$31.5 billion, other liabilities of \$14.5 billion and minority interest brings the right-hand side to \$102.7 billion, which means the operating assets are being valued by the market at far more than their book value.^[Benninga, *Financial Modeling*, ch. 2, pp. 58–59.] A DCF valuation is a way of asking whether that market value is justified by the cash the operating assets can produce.

### 1.5 A valuation is a story turned into numbers {.unnumbered}

The inputs in the following sections are not independent. Revenue growth, the operating margin, the amount of capital needed to support growth and the risk of the business all describe one business. A good valuation starts with a narrative about that business (how big the market is, what share the firm can win, why competitors cannot copy it, how profitable it can become) and then translates each sentence into an input. Every number must trace back to a sentence in the story, and every sentence about the future should show up in a number.^[Damodaran, valuation course slides, Spring 2023, Session 10, "Estimating Growth and Reinvestment," <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/podcasts/valspr23/session10slides.pdf>.]

### 1.6 Example Co.: the starting point {.unnumbered}

Example Co. is valued in Sections 2 to 6. Its base year (from @sec-fsa) is:

| **Example Co. base year (\$)** | **Amount** | **Note** |
|---------------------------------|------------|-------------------------|
| Revenues | 1,000 | |
| Operating income (EBIT) | 150 | 15.0% operating margin |
| Tax rate | 30% | |
| After-tax operating income (NOPAT) | 105 | 150 × (1 – 0.30) |
| Debt | 400 | Book value, used as a proxy for market value |
| Cash | 100 | |
| Shareholders' equity (book) | 600 | |
| Invested capital | 900 | Debt + equity – cash |
| Return on invested capital (ROIC) | 11.7% | 105 ÷ 900 |

### Check your understanding {.unnumbered}

1.  Why is a dollar of cash flow received in year 1 worth more than a dollar received in year 8, and what could make up for the delay?

2.  A firm pays 40% of its free cash flow to equity as dividends. Which of the three approaches in 1.3 is least likely to be reliable?

3.  An analyst discounts free cash flow to the firm at the cost of equity and then subtracts debt. Does she over- or understate equity value? (Answer: understates it, because the cost of equity is higher than WACC. In the example above the error is \$260.)

4.  For which kinds of company would you prefer firm valuation to equity valuation, and why?

5.  Caterpillar's market-based enterprise value is \$102.7 billion against \$59.5 billion on book values. Name two reasons the two might differ that have nothing to do with market mispricing.

## Section 2. Free Cash Flow to the Firm {.unnumbered}

### Learning objectives {.unnumbered}

- Compute free cash flow to the firm from the income statement and from the cash flow statement.

- Explain why operating income is taxed as if the firm had no debt.

- Define reinvestment and the reinvestment rate.

- Adjust reported operating income for leases, research spending and one-time items.

- Choose between the effective and marginal tax rate, including firms with tax-loss carryforwards.

- Distinguish FCFF from FCFE and explain why FCFF can be positive while FCFE is negative.

### 2.1 The definition {.unnumbered}

**Free cash flow to the firm** is the cash the operating business produces for all of its capital providers, measured before any payment to lenders or shareholders and after the investment needed to sustain the business:^[Damodaran, *The Little Book of Valuation*, companion page "Cash Flows," <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/littlebook/cashflows.htm>; Benninga, *Financial Modeling*, ch. 2, pp. 60–62.]

$$
\text{FCFF} = \text{EBIT}(1-t) - (\text{Capital expenditures} - \text{Depreciation} + \Delta\text{Non-cash working capital})
$$

The bracket is **reinvestment**: net capital expenditure plus the change in operating working capital. Dividing it by after-tax operating income gives the **reinvestment rate**, so that

$$
\text{FCFF} = \text{EBIT}(1-t)\,(1 - \text{Reinvestment rate})
$$

The reinvestment rate can be above 100% for a firm investing heavily and negative for one that is shrinking its asset base.

The same number can be reached from the net income side. Starting with profit after tax, add back depreciation and other non-cash expenses, subtract the increase in operating current assets and capital expenditure, add the increase in operating current liabilities, and then **add back after-tax net interest** so that financing does not affect the answer:

| **Income statement route** | **EBIT route** |
|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| Profit after taxes | EBIT × (1 – tax rate) |
| + Depreciation and other non-cash expenses | + Depreciation and other non-cash expenses |
| – Increase in operating current assets | – Increase in operating current assets |
| + Increase in operating current liabilities | + Increase in operating current liabilities |
| – Capital expenditure | – Capital expenditure |
| + After-tax interest on debt, – after-tax interest on cash | |

"Operating" matters. Cash, marketable securities, short-term debt and the current portion of long-term debt are financing items, not working capital, and are left out of the working capital change.^[Benninga, *Financial Modeling*, ch. 2, pp. 61–62.] A rise in receivables is a cash drain that the income statement ignores, and a rise in payables is a source of cash.

#### Why operating income is taxed as if there were no debt {.unnumbered}

FCFF is computed on EBIT taxed at the full rate, as though the firm had no debt. The tax saving from interest is not in the cash flow. It is in the discount rate, through the after-tax cost of debt in WACC (Section 3). Counting it in both places would double count it.^[Damodaran, "Cash Flows," <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/littlebook/cashflows.htm>.]

#### Illustration {.unnumbered}

A firm has EBIT of 200, a tax rate of 25%, capital expenditure of 80, depreciation of 50 and a 10 increase in working capital. After-tax operating income is 200 × 0.75 = 150. Reinvestment is 80 – 50 + 10 = 40, so FCFF = 150 – 40 = 110. The reinvestment rate is 40 ÷ 150 = 26.7%, and 150 × (1 – 0.267) = 110.

### 2.2 Taxes {.unnumbered}

Two rates are available: the **effective** rate (taxes paid divided by taxable income) and the **marginal** rate (the rate on the next dollar of income). For a firm with high-tax and low-tax income the effective rate can be well below the marginal rate for years, and it can be erratic. A well-known example is Merck, whose reported tax rate was 14.8% in 2009, 40.6% in 2010 and 12.8% in 2011. The 2010 spike came in a low-income year in which tax planning evidently failed to work, so a forecast based on the two good years would use a rate near 13% to 15%.^[Benninga, *Financial Modeling*, ch. 3, pp. 75–76.]

The practical rule is to start the forecast at the effective rate and move it toward the marginal rate over the forecast period, so that the terminal value is taxed at the marginal rate. Using the marginal rate from the start understates early after-tax income; carrying the effective rate forever overstates later value, because tax advantages do not last forever.^[Damodaran, valuation course slides, Spring 2023, Session 8, "Estimating Cash Flows," <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/podcasts/valspr23/session8slides.pdf>.]

#### Firms with tax-loss carryforwards {.unnumbered}

Take a firm with \$1,000 million of net operating losses carried forward, EBIT of \$500 million a year for three years and a 40% marginal rate. The carryforward shelters all \$500 million in years 1 and 2, so taxes are zero and after-tax operating income is \$500 million. By year 3 the carryforward is used up, so the full \$500 million is taxed at 40%: taxes are \$200 million and after-tax operating income is \$300 million. The benefit is real, but it is temporary and must be removed from the terminal value.^[Damodaran, Session 8 slides, <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/podcasts/valspr23/session8slides.pdf>.]

### 2.3 Reinvestment {.unnumbered}

Growth is not free. To grow, a firm must add working capital, plants, equipment and, for many firms today, less tangible assets. Net capital expenditure is capital expenditure minus depreciation. It depends on growth, so it cannot be forecast independently of the growth assumption (Section 4). Two cautions apply when looking at history:

- **Normalize the base year.** One year of capital expenditure can be unrepresentative. A firm that spent very little in the base year will show a flattering FCFF that cannot be sustained, and a firm that made a large acquisition will show the opposite. In both cases, average over several years or build the figure from the growth plan.^[Damodaran, "Common errors in DCF valuation," 2011 NYIF presentation, <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/pdfiles/country/TenErrorsNYIF2011.pdf>.]

- **Include acquisitions when growth depends on them.** Net capital expenditure for a firm that grows by buying other firms is net capex plus acquisitions, less the amortization of past acquisitions, normalized over time.^[Damodaran, Session 8 slides, <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/podcasts/valspr23/session8slides.pdf>.]

### 2.4 Cleaning the operating income {.unnumbered}

Accounting statements are the starting point for valuation, but they classify some items in ways that distort operating income and invested capital. The main adjustments are:

| **Item** | **Accounting treatment** | **Valuation treatment** |
|-----------------|------------------------|------------------------------|
| Operating leases | Since 2019, recorded as a lease liability and an asset (see @sec-fsa) | Treat the lease liability as debt, discounted at the firm's pre-tax cost of debt; add the interest component back to operating income |
| Research and development | Expensed as incurred | Capitalize: treat as an investment, amortize over its useful life and add the resulting asset to invested capital |
| Stock-based compensation | Expensed, then added back in the cash flow statement because no cash leaves | Treat as a real expense; do not add it back |
| One-time items | Reported separately, sometimes recurring every year | Remove only if truly one time; a charge that recurs every few years is part of normal earnings |
| Cyclical or distressed margins | Reflect the current year | Normalize toward the average through the cycle, or toward the industry average for firms with structural problems |

#### Leases {.unnumbered}

If lease payments are fixed commitments much like interest, a lease is financing, and the part of the lease expense that is effectively interest should be removed from operating expenses. The treatment is to discount the future commitments at the firm's pre-tax cost of unsecured debt, treat that present value as debt, and add the lease expense back to operating income. (The simple method adds the current-year lease expense to EBIT; a fuller method adds back only the imputed interest and the depreciation of the leased asset.) Leaving operating leases off the balance sheet lowered EBIT by the whole lease expense but left debt and capital understated, so return on capital and return on equity looked too high and the debt ratio looked too low.^[Damodaran, "Dealing with Operating Leases and R&D in Valuation," valuation Q&A, <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/valquestions/opler&d.htm>; and Session 8 slides (2023), <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/podcasts/valspr23/session8slides.pdf>.]

#### Research and development {.unnumbered}

Accounting expenses R&D immediately even though it is meant to produce future revenue. To capitalize it, pick an amortizable life (two to ten years), gather R&D for that many past years, and count the unamortized portion of each year's spending. With a five-year life the current year counts at 100%, the prior year at 80%, and so on down to 20% for four years ago.^[Damodaran, Session 8 slides, <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/podcasts/valspr23/session8slides.pdf>.]

SAP illustrates the effect (€ millions, five-year life):

| **SAP, € millions** | **As reported** | **R&D capitalized** |
|--------------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| R&D expense in the year | 1,020 | (reclassified) |
| Amortization of the research asset | — | 903 |
| Operating income | 2,025 | 2,142 (= 2,025 + 1,020 – 903) |
| Research asset added to book equity | — | 2,914 |
| Return on capital | about 30% | about 19% |

Adding back the R&D and subtracting the amortization raises operating income by €117 million, but net capital expenditure rises by the same amount, so FCFF is unchanged. What changes is the picture of the business: invested capital is much larger, return on capital is lower, and the reinvestment rate needed to explain growth is higher.

#### Stock-based compensation {.unnumbered}

The operating section of the cash flow statement adds back stock-based pay because no cash leaves the firm. The shortcut of accepting the operating cash flows as reported therefore keeps that add-back.^[Benninga, *Financial Modeling*, ch. 2, pp. 63–64.] This chapter does not: shares or options given to employees are a cost borne by existing shareholders, so the expense stays in operating income.

#### Normalizing {.unnumbered}

Replace a one-time charge only if it is truly one time. For earnings that move with commodity prices or recessions, use an average across the cycle. For a young company, target the margin that mature firms in the business earn and move toward it. For a company with structural problems, target the industry average and move toward it as the problems are fixed.^[Damodaran, Session 8 slides, <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/podcasts/valspr23/session8slides.pdf>.] The warning signs listed in @sec-fsa (income from unspecified sources, falling SG&A or R&D as a share of revenue, accrual earnings running ahead of cash earnings) apply here too, because a distorted base year distorts every year that follows.

### 2.5 From the cash flow statement to FCFF {.unnumbered}

The consolidated statement of cash flows already contains most of what is needed. The procedure is:^[Benninga, *Financial Modeling*, ch. 2, pp. 63–66, and ch. 4, pp. 121–122.]

1.  Accept the operating cash flows as reported (after the stock-based pay adjustment above).

2.  Keep investing cash flows tied to operations (capital expenditure, proceeds from selling equipment) and delete purchases and sales of financial securities.

3.  Ignore all financing cash flows (debt issued or repaid, stock issued or repurchased, dividends).

4. Remove items that will not recur.

5.  Add back after-tax net interest, so that financing does not affect the result.

ABC Corp., a teaching example, shows the conversion (in thousands of dollars):

| **ABC Corp.** | **2008** | **2009** | **2010** | **2011** | **2012** |
|-----------------|----------|----------|----------|----------|----------|
| Net cash provided by operating activities | 470,116 | 611,160 | 574,747 | 592,844 | 616,505 |
| Purchases of property, plant and equipment | (48,944) | (70,326) | (89,947) | (37,044) | (88,426) |
| Proceeds from disposing of property, plant and equipment | 197 | 6,956 | 22,942 | 6,179 | 28,693 |
| Free cash flow before interest adjustment | 416,369 | 492,790 | 507,742 | 561,979 | 556,772 |
| Add back after-tax net interest | 54,537 | 61,658 | 44,271 | 36,620 | 36,504 |
| **Free cash flow (FCF)** | **470,906** | **554,448** | **552,013** | **598,599** | **593,276** |

(Short-term investments are removed from the investing section, as they are financial.) The five-year history shows FCF in a fairly stable range, which is a useful guide for a short-term projection, though a firm whose history is erratic needs a model built from its drivers (Section 4).

### 2.6 FCFF and FCFE compared {.unnumbered}

| **Feature** | **FCFE** | **FCFF** |
|----------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Starting point | Net income (after interest) | After-tax operating income (before interest) |
| Taxes | Already in net income | Computed as if the firm had no debt |
| Debt flows | Net debt repaid or issued is subtracted or added | Not included |
| Claimants | Equity only | All capital providers |
| Discount rate | Cost of equity | Cost of capital |
| Can be negative? | Yes: losses, heavy reinvestment, or debt repayment | Yes, but not because of debt repayment |

A highly levered firm that is paying down debt can show positive FCFF and negative FCFE at the same time. FCFE is, in effect, FCFF minus after-tax interest minus net debt repayment. When FCFF is negative the firm must raise new capital, in a mix set by the weights in the cost of capital.^[Damodaran, "Cash Flows," <https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/littlebook/cashflows.htm>.]

### 2.7 Example Co.: base year free cash flow {.unnumbered}

Example Co. has NOPAT of 105. Its invested capital is 900 and its revenue is 1,000, so each dollar of invested capital supports 1,000 ÷ 900 = \$1.11 of sales. Section 4 turns this relationship into a reinvestment forecast. For now, note two things: after-tax operating income is 10.5% of revenue, and a firm earning 11.7% on capital must reinvest about two-thirds of its after-tax operating income (8% ÷ 11.7% ≈ 68%) to grow at 8%.

### Check your understanding {.unnumbered}

1.  Why are cash and short-term debt excluded from the working capital change in FCFF?

2.  A firm has EBIT of 300, a 30% tax rate, capital expenditure of 140, depreciation of 90 and a 20 rise in working capital. Compute FCFF and the reinvestment rate. (Answer: after-tax operating income = 210; reinvestment = 140 – 90 + 20 = 70; FCFF = 140; reinvestment rate = 70 ÷ 210 = 33.3%.)

3.  A firm's interest tax shield is included in the after-tax cost of debt. Why is operating income still taxed as if there were no debt?

4.  A software firm spends 500 a year on R&D. Which two figures change when R&D is capitalized, and which one does not? (Answer: operating income and invested capital change; FCFF does not.)

5.  A firm has 600 of net operating losses and EBIT of 400 a year with a 40% marginal rate. What are after-tax operating income in years 1 and 2? (Answer: year 1 has no tax, so 400. In year 2, 200 of losses remain, so taxable income is 200, tax is 80 and after-tax operating income is 320.)

6.  Why must a terminal value not include the benefit of a tax-loss carryforward?

7.  A firm's FCF history is 470, 554, 552, 599 and 593. What would you check before projecting forward from this range?
